plot.label: Mass of a radioactive isotope remaining over 60 years, falling by half every 10 years, invented data for practice

items.q: What is the fuel in a nuclear power plant?
options: Water, which is split apart to release its energy
Steam, which carries the energy to the turbine
Coal, which is burned to heat the reactor core
Uranium, enriched to a higher share of uranium-235

why.correct: The fuel is uranium (usually enriched to about 3 to 5 percent uranium-235). Water and steam only carry the heat to the turbine.
options: Water is the coolant and the source of steam; it is not split for energy.
Steam carries heat; it is not the fuel.
No fuel is burned in a nuclear reactor.
Right: uranium-235 is the fuel.

items.q: What happens during nuclear fission in a reactor?
options: Uranium burns in oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide and a lot of heat
Water molecules in the core break apart into hydrogen and oxygen
A neutron splits a U-235 nucleus, freeing heat and neutrons
Two hydrogen nuclei join to form one helium nucleus, releasing heat

why.correct: A neutron strikes a uranium-235 nucleus, which splits into smaller nuclei, releasing a large amount of heat and 2 or 3 neutrons that can split more nuclei: a chain reaction.
options: Fission is not burning and releases no carbon dioxide.
Splitting water is a chemical change, not a nuclear one.
Right: splitting heavy nuclei is fission.
Joining light nuclei is fusion, which powers the sun, not today's reactors.

items.q: What do the control rods in a reactor do?
options: They store the spent fuel after it is removed from the core
They absorb neutrons, which slows the chain reaction
They add extra uranium to the core when the reaction slows down
They carry the heat from the reactor core out to the turbine

why.correct: Control rods are made of materials that absorb neutrons. Lowering them in takes neutrons out of the chain reaction; pulling them out lets it speed up.
options: Spent fuel is stored in pools and casks, not in control rods.
Right: absorbing neutrons controls the rate.
Fuel rods hold the uranium; control rods do not add fuel.
Water carries the heat.

items.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for half of a sample's radioactive atoms to decay
Half the time it takes for the whole sample to decay away
The length of time a sample stays dangerous to people nearby
The age at which a sample weighs half as much as at the start

why.correct: In each half-life, half of the remaining radioactive atoms decay. After two half-lives a quarter is left, after three an eighth.
options: Right: half the atoms decay in one half-life.
Decay never quite reaches zero; each half-life halves what is left.
How long a sample is dangerous depends on many half-lives and the type of radiation.
Half-life counts atoms that decay; the decay products still have mass.

items.q: A sample holds 200 g of cesium-137, which has a half-life of about 30 years. How many grams of cesium-137 remain after 90 years?

mistakes.why: You divided by the number of half-lives. Halve the amount once for each half-life: 200 → 100 → 50 → 25.
That is after one half-life (30 years). Ninety years is three half-lives.
That is how much has decayed. The question asks how much remains.

items.q: A hospital receives 80 mg of iodine-131, which has a half-life of 8 days. Write the setup for the amount left after 24 days, then give the answer.

why.correct: $80\,\text{mg} \times 0.5^{24/8} = 80 \times 0.5^{3} = 80 \times 0.125 = 10\,\text{mg}$. Writing $0.5^{3}$ directly (24 ÷ 8 = 3 half-lives) earns the setup too.

mistakes.why: Halving is repeated, so the number of half-lives (24 ÷ 8 = 3) is an exponent: 0.5^(24/8).
Dividing by 3 is not three halvings. Use 80 × 0.5^3.
That is 80 × 0.5 × 1.5. Each half-life halves the amount: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10.
You subtracted the 10 mg left from 80. Report what remains, not what decayed.

items.q: Strontium-90 has a half-life of about 29 years. How many years until a spill of strontium-90 falls to one sixteenth of its starting amount?

why.correct: One sixteenth is $(\tfrac{1}{2})^{4}$, so 4 half-lives: $4 \times 29 = 116$ years.

mistakes.why: One sixteenth is 4 halvings (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16), not 16. Multiply 4 by 29.
Eight half-lives would leave 1/256. Count halvings: 1/16 takes 4.

items.q: According to the graph, what is the half-life of this isotope?
options: 10 years
20 years
400 years
60 years

why.correct: The amount falls from 800 g to 400 g, half, in 10 years.
options: Right: 800 g becomes 400 g after 10 years.
After 20 years only a quarter (200 g) is left.
400 is the mass after one half-life, not a time.
Sixty years is six half-lives.

items.q: How many grams of the isotope remain after 40 years?

mistakes.why: You divided by the number of half-lives. Halve four times: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50.
That is how much decayed. The question asks how much is left.

items.q: Which statement describes the shape of the curve?
options: The mass lost each decade grows larger as the sample ages
The isotope has decayed away after two half-lives pass
The mass lost each decade shrinks as less remains
The same mass of the isotope is lost in each decade

why.correct: Each half-life removes half of what is left: 400 g, then 200 g, then 100 g. The curve flattens but does not reach zero.
options: The losses shrink, they do not grow.
After two half-lives a quarter (200 g) is still left.
Right: half of a smaller amount each time.
A straight line would lose the same mass each decade; this curve does not.

items.q: Spent fuel contains isotopes with half-lives from days to tens of thousands of years. What does this mean for storing it?
options: It can be burned to remove the radioactivity
It must be kept isolated from people for thousands of years
It can be released after a few months, once short-lived isotopes decay
It becomes safe after one half-life of its longest-lived isotope

why.correct: Long-lived isotopes such as plutonium-239 (half-life about 24,000 years) stay dangerous for many half-lives, so storage must last thousands of years.
options: Burning does not change radioactive decay.
Right: long half-lives demand very long storage.
Long-lived isotopes remain after the short-lived ones decay.
After one half-life, half of that isotope is still there.

items.q: In the diagram, what is the source of the heat that makes steam?
options: Fission of uranium-235 in the fuel rods
Burning coal under the reactor
The cooling tower
The generator

why.correct: Fission in the fuel rods releases the heat; water carries it to the steam generator.
options: Right: fission in the fuel rods.
Nothing is burned in a nuclear reactor.
The cooling tower removes heat; it does not supply it.
The generator makes electricity from motion.

items.q: Operators lower the control rods fully into the core. What happens next?
options: More fissions occur, so the reactor makes more steam
The uranium in the fuel rods turns into coal and stops reacting
Steam flow to the turbine stays the same as before
Fewer fissions occur, so less heat and electricity

why.correct: More neutrons are absorbed, the chain reaction slows or stops, less heat is made and the turbine slows.
options: Lowering the rods slows fission; it does not speed it up.
Uranium does not turn into coal.
With less heat, less steam reaches the turbine.
Right: absorbing neutrons slows the reaction.

items.q: Based on the diagram, why can losing the supply of cooling water lead to a meltdown, even after the control rods stop fission?
options: The turbine sends heat back into the core
The cooling tower adds heat when it runs dry
Decay of fission products keeps heating the fuel
The control rods start making heat once they are lowered

why.correct: Radioactive fission products keep giving off heat after the reaction stops. Without cooling water, the fuel overheats and can melt, as at Fukushima in 2011.
options: Heat flows from the core to the turbine, not back.
A dry cooling tower removes less heat; it does not add any.
Right: decay heat continues after shutdown.
Control rods absorb neutrons; they do not make heat.

items.q: Describe one environmental advantage and one disadvantage of the nuclear plant in the diagram compared with a coal plant.

why.correct: Advantage: no carbon dioxide or smoke while running, because nothing is burned. Disadvantage: radioactive spent fuel that must be stored for thousands of years, or the risk of an accident.

specific.frame: An advantage is ___ because ___. A disadvantage is ___.

adv.label: Advantage
options: no carbon dioxide is released while it runs
it uses a renewable fuel
it makes no waste

why.1: Uranium is a mined, nonrenewable fuel.

how.label: Why
options: fission releases heat without burning any fuel
the cooling tower removes carbon dioxide
uranium absorbs carbon dioxide

why.1: Cooling towers release water vapor and heat; they do not remove carbon dioxide.
why.2: Uranium does not absorb carbon dioxide.

dis.label: Disadvantage
options: radioactive spent fuel must be stored safely for thousands of years
it releases large amounts of smoke
its fuel is water, which is running out

why.1: A nuclear plant burns nothing, so it releases no smoke.
why.2: The fuel is uranium; water only carries the heat.

specific.model: An advantage is that no carbon dioxide is released while it runs, because fission releases heat without burning fuel. A disadvantage is that the radioactive spent fuel must be stored safely for thousands of years.

items.q: Which event is an example of a nuclear accident that released radioactive material over a wide area?
options: The 1986 Chernobyl explosion and fire in Ukraine
An oil tanker running aground near Alaska
A coal mine collapse in West Virginia
A dam failure that flooded a valley

why.correct: At Chernobyl a reactor exploded and burned, spreading radioactive material across much of Europe. Three Mile Island (1979) and Fukushima (2011) were also meltdowns.
options: Right: Chernobyl was the worst nuclear accident.
A tanker grounding is a petroleum accident.
A mine collapse is a coal mining accident.
A dam failure is a hazard of dams, not of nuclear plants.

items.q: Why must uranium ore be enriched before it is used as reactor fuel?
options: Natural uranium is far too radioactive for workers to handle safely
Enrichment turns the mined uranium into a renewable fuel
Enrichment removes the carbon from uranium so that it burns cleanly
Natural uranium has too little U-235 to keep fission going

why.correct: Natural uranium is about 0.7 percent uranium-235. Most reactors need fuel with about 3 to 5 percent to keep the chain reaction going.
options: Natural uranium is weakly radioactive; enrichment raises its uranium-235 share.
Uranium is mined from a fixed supply; enrichment does not change that.
Uranium is not burned and contains no carbon.
Right: the fissile isotope must be concentrated.
